original_value: Sociotechnical imaginaries are futures that people envision might be possible and desirable. They have a real impact on how systems are designed and what values they have embedded in their design. This article examines imaginaries about autonomous systems, decentralized systems, and decentralized autonomous systems. Through a discussion of the literature on autonomous and decentralized systems and how these imaginaries play out in the blockchain community based on my qualitative research, I demonstrate how decentralized autonomous systems are related to imaginaries about the organization of and the future of work. I identify three framings of imaginaries about autonomous systems: (1) autonomous technology as physical objects, (2) as mathematical rules, and (3) as artificial mangers. I also identify two sometimes conflicting framings of imaginaries about distributed and decentralized technology: these technologies as a new form of production and as freedom from control. These imaginaries intersect in decentralized autonomous systems, and I examine what they can tell us about the design and governance of such technologies. Lastly, I suggest ways of using the concept of imaginaries in participatory design.

This article explores imaginaries surrounding autonomous systems, decentralized systems, and decentralized autonomous systems. Drawing on literature about autonomous and decentralized systems, as well as qualitative research on how these imaginaries appear in the blockchain community, I show how decentralized autonomous systems connect to ideas about the organization of work and its future. I identify three ways autonomous systems are framed: as physical objects, as mathematical rules, and as artificial managers. I also identify two sometimes conflicting framings of distributed and decentralized technology: as a new form of production and as freedom from control. These imaginaries converge in decentralized autonomous systems, and I consider what they reveal about the design and governance of such technologies. Finally, I propose ways to use the concept of imaginaries in participatory design.
